newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish forex intervention modest since March - C.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Irish forex intervention modest since March - C.Bank.

text.p: The Central Bank of Ireland said on Thursday that its intervention in foreign exchange markets had been modest since end-March.
"Intervention by the bank to smooth foreign-exchange market movements was modest in the period from end-March to end-August," the central bank said in its quarterly bulletin.

It noted that the overall value of the Irish pound, as measured by the trade-weighted index, had risen by two percent in the first eight months of the year, and had moved up significantly within the ERM (Exchange Rate Mechanism) band.
Officials said the aim of government exchange rate policy was to trade comfortably in the ERM band but denied that the bank was trying to keep the Irish pound in a one-percent range against the mark.
"There's no such thing as a set numerical," one official said at a news conference to release the bank's quarterly bulletin.

Officials also said they did not see the gap between Irish and German short-term rates as a problem. The differential widened after Irish wholesale rates tightened in June and the Bundesbank cut its repo rate in August.
"I don't see that that is a problem as such given relative growth rates," assistant general director Michael Casey said.
Officials said short-term interest rates were regarded as a monetary instrument, used to accomodate local conditions.
A significant positive gap between Irish and German rates was to be expected as the two economies are at very different stages in the economic cycle.
They also noted that the Maastricht criteria for Economic and Monetary Union related only to the differential in long-term interest rates.
They said the Irish yield curve was quite flat and long-term interest rates were low with Irish 10-year bond yields trading 110 basis points above their German equivalent.
